ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The cervical vertebrae are the seven upper spinal bones that support the head, protect the spinal cord, and enable neck movement. Their unique anatomy creates landmarks for vascular and neural structures, making them crucial in trauma and disease.

sections.p: The cervical spine consists of seven vertebrae (C1‑C7) that form the neck, bear the skull’s weight, and allow flexion, extension, rotation, and lateral bending.
b: C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) are specialized for rotation
C3‑C6 have a typical vertebral body, transverse foramen, and spinous process
C7 often has a prominent spinous process (vertebra prominens)

sections.p: Each cervical vertebra has a small body, a vertebral foramen forming the spinal canal, transverse foramina for the vertebral arteries, and articulations for the skull and ribs.
b: Transverse foramen: passage for vertebral artery, vein, sympathetic chain
Uncinate processes (C3‑C7) guide flexion/extension
Facet orientation: oblique, allowing rotation

sections.p: Anteriorly lie the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid; laterally the carotid sheath; posteriorly the deep neck muscles and spinal cord.
b: Vertebral artery ascends through transverse foramina to brain
Sympathetic chain runs on vertebral bodies
Cervical plexus emerges between anterior scalene and levator scapulae

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from the vertebral arteries (through transverse foramina) and segmental branches of the ascending cervical artery.
b: Vertebral artery supplies the posterior spinal cord
Ascending cervical artery supplies muscles and posterior elements

sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the dorsal rami; motor innervation to neck muscles comes from ventral rami of cervical spinal nerves (C1‑C8).
b: C1‑C2 dorsal rami supply skin over the posterior neck
C3‑C4 ventral rami form the phrenic nerve (C3‑C5)

sections.p: Provides structural support for the head, protects the cervical spinal cord, and enables a wide range of neck movements essential for airway protection and visual scanning.
b: Supports skull weight (~4‑5 kg)
Allows 80° rotation each side
Facilitates swallowing and respiration via muscle attachments

sections.p: Cervical vertebrae are vulnerable to fracture, dislocation, and degenerative disease, which can compromise the spinal cord, vertebral artery, or airway.
b: Hangman's fracture (C2 pars fracture) – high‑energy trauma
Odontoid (dens) fracture – common in elderly falls
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy – progressive cord compression
Vertebral artery dissection – can follow neck manipulation

t.b: Detects gross fractures or dislocations; if unavailable, use clinical C‑spine immobilisation and refer
Defines fracture lines and canal compromise; essential when radiograph equivocal
Assesses cord edema, ligament injury, and disc herniation; if MRI not available, treat as unstable fracture based on CT
Screens for dissection when MRI/MRA unavailable; abnormal flow suggests injury

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: C1 has no body; C2 has odontoid process (dens)
Palpate C7 spinous process as a landmark for cervical level
Assess for neck pain, tenderness, neurological deficits, and airway compromise

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neck pain with neurological deficit (weakness, numbness)
Progressive weakness or loss of sensation in arms or legs
Signs of vertebral artery injury (neck pain, Horner syndrome, posterior circulation stroke)
Respiratory distress from cervical spine instability

faq.q: Why is the transverse foramen important?
faq.a: It carries the vertebral artery, which supplies the posterior brain; injury can cause stroke.

faq.q: What makes C1 and C2 different from other cervical vertebrae?
faq.a: C1 lacks a body and spinous process; C2 has the odontoid process that articulates with C1 for rotation.

faq.q: How can you clinically assess cervical spine stability?
faq.a: Look for tenderness, step-off, neurological signs, and use the NEXUS or Canadian C‑Spine rules to decide imaging.

exam: Identify C1‑C7 on a lateral cervical spine X‑ray and name a key distinguishing feature of each.
Explain the mechanism and clinical consequences of an odontoid fracture.
Describe the steps in managing a suspected vertebral artery dissection after neck trauma.
